items.excerpt: Voting ends in Brazil's presidential runoff after 2-hour extension Voting in Brazil's presidential runoff ended at 7 p.m. Brasilia time (2200 GMT) on Sunday, two hours later than originally scheduled, following a Supreme Federal Court ruling extending voting hours amid disruptions caused by public transportation problems and heavy rains in several parts of the country. Results of the closely contested runoff were expected within hours of the close of voting. Serbia's Vucic concedes election defeat as student-led movement claims victory Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Sunday's snap parliamentary election, as independent projections and leaders of a student-backed movement born out of anti-corruption protests confirmed an outright parliamentary majority that ends the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year grip on power. Initial projections released by polling agencies Ipsos and CeSID showed the "Student List -- Students Win" winning 52 percent of the vote, well ahead of Vucic's SNS-led coalition, "Aleksandar Vucic -- United Serbia," which stood at 39.3 percent. Bulgaria's incumbent president leads presidential election, but runoff required Bulgaria's incumbent President Iliana Iotova is leading in the country's presidential election on Sunday, but a runoff will be required to determine the winner, according to exit polls. According to the exit poll by Alpha Research, Iotova is expected to get 35.3 percent of the valid votes, while the exit poll by Myara Sociology Agency showed that Iotova would get 35.2 percent. Nigeria identifies 53 contacts linked to confirmed Ebola case Nigerian public health authorities on Sunday said they had identified and followed up on 53 contacts linked to the country's only confirmed Ebola case. Jide Idris, director-general of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, told a media briefing Sunday evening that the contacts include healthcare workers, domestic staff, and the patient's spouse. At least 20 seriously injured in bus accident in Spain's Barcelona province At least 20 people were seriously injured in a bus accident in Spain's northeastern province of Barcelona on Sunday, according to Catalonia's Medical Emergency System. The accident occurred on the BV-5114 road in the municipality of Fogars de Montclus, where a bus reportedly plunged down an embankment. Bus-truck crash kills at least 22 in SE Kenya At least 22 people were killed and six others injured on Sunday morning following a head-on collision between a passenger bus and a truck along the Nairobi-Mombasa highway in southeastern Kenya. Makueni County Commissioner Abdullahi Khalif confirmed that the crash, which involved a tipper truck and a bus carrying 45 passengers, occurred at about 7:45 a.m. (0445 GMT) in the Kanga area. ■

items.title: Fed survey shows price pressures intensifying amid rise in fuel costs By Reuters
items.excerpt: Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US labor market remained stuck in a low-hire, low-fire state and inflation was intensifying across parts of the country in recent weeks, a Federal Reserve report showed on Wednesday, underscoring what’s at stake as the central bank weighs whether to deliver a second straight interest rate hike later this month. While businesses in much of the country have a positive outlook, their "expectations tend to be for slight growth, weighted toward manufacturing and burdened by persistent uncertainties," the Fed said in its latest "Beige Book" report, a compendium of survey-based data and commentary from businesses compiled by its 12 regional banks to provide a read on economic conditions. "Firms reported elevated diesel prices and noted that fuel surcharges were passing on increased costs throughout the supply chain," said the report. It noted that three of the Fed’s 12 districts described price growth as robust and eight as moderate, with three noting it was "intensifying." "Contacts in multiple Districts also noted continued price pressure from other commodities, tariffs, and insurance," it said. The survey also acts as something of a barometer for the economic pressures voters are dealing with ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine whether President Donald Trump’s Republican Party maintains control of Congress. ... Financial markets are pricing about a 37% chance of a rate hike at the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting after data on Wednesday showed consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, far faster than the central bank’s 2% target and above the consensus forecast of economists polled by Reuters. Higher gasoline costs from the Middle East war were largely to blame for the higher CPI reading, with fast-rising software and toy prices also pointing to the impact of AI-driven demand and higher tariffs under Trump’s trade policy. The rising cost of borrowing to buy a home is an added burden for many US households. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose last week to 7.5%, the highest in nearly three years, the Mortgage Bankers Association said on Wednesday.

The Department ‌of Justice’s lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump’s administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers. At the end of the two-hour oral argument, Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to rule as quickly as possible. items.excerpt: With the US midterms just over a week away US President Donald Trump has launched another fierce anti-Muslim attack on Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. El-Sayed’s race against Republican Mike Rogers could help determine control of the US Senate.

President Donald Trump’s net approval rating improved 3 percentage points over the past week, with 46% approving and 51% disapproving in our latest tracker update. That improvement comes as the federal government’s Oct. 1 shutdown remains our most salient story for the third week in a row. It’s just the latest indication that, as we get into more below, the impasse on Capitol Hill may be full of sound and fury, but signifies nothing for the average voter. 36% Just over a third of voters said Trump should prioritize deportations of undocumented immigrants, in line with our findings since before his militarized campaign against illegal immigration in major cities began in August as his approval rating on the matter has rebounded from recent lows. The administration is on track to shatter the annual record for the number of undocumented immigrants deported from the United States, Fox News notes. 23% Less than a quarter of voters have seen, read or heard “a lot” about Trump’s construction of a new $250 million ballroom at the White House, but that might soon increase. As The Washington Post reported yesterday under a striking image shared by a source, demolition crews began ripping down part of the presidential mansion’s East Wing despite Trump’s pledge that the pending 90,000-square-foot structure wouldn’t interfere or touch the existing building. Shutdown Trump is set to host Senate Republicans for lunch at the White House today “to celebrate their unity in the government shutdown fight and for passing nominees,” according to Politico, which noted that the party’s push for a Nov. 21 funding extension may need to change as Washington gets closer to the expiration date. Some conservatives are said to be pushing for a continuing resolution that would run until March or even next October, though the idea irks Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine). Perhaps most notably: NOTUS reports that some Republican senators — even Collins herself — are beginning to entertain the idea of employing the nuclear option to pass a continuing resolution with a simple majority. On the Obamacare front, Politico also reports that Republicans are ramping up talks with the White House on what kind of premium tax credit expansion the party could support once the government is reopened. The party is said to be considering a year-end health care policy package with a two-year extension of scaled-back ACA subsidies though it’s uncertain how that would be received in the House. Nominees The New York Times reports that Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is among at least four Republican senators who have come out in opposition to Trump’s nomination of Paul Ingrassia to lead the Office of Special Counsel following a Politico report documenting a series of racist text messages. That’s enough Republicans to kill Ingrassia’s nomination even before his planned testimony to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. Separately, Axios noted that Trump has paused the nomination of former Florida Deputy Attorney General John Guard to fill an open open judicial seat in the Middle District of Florida over his connection with a criminal probe, and The Wall Street Journal points out a “power struggle” between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Elon Musk-aligned billionaire Jared Isaacman over the stewardship of NASA. Gerrymandering House Democratic leaders in Washington have devised a new congressional boundary map for Illinois that would target Republican Rep. Darin LaHood, aiming to reduce the state’s GOP-leaning districts to two, Punchbowl News reports on the party’s response to GOP gerrymandering efforts. Legislators will be in a veto session next week, but will have to move fast ahead of Illinois' pending filing deadline or move next year’s primary date. U.S.-China Trump has rolled out a list of topics he expects to discuss when he meets next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in South Korea. He pointed to rare earth minerals, fentanyl, soybeans and Taiwan, “underlining the divisive topics the two sides plan to tackle at the negotiating table as a fragile trade truce nears its expiration,” as Bloomberg News put it.
